gl: belonging to a herd; feeding at large
d: belonging to a herd; feeding at large

e.t: This adjective describes something belonging to a herd or feeding at large. It points to animals understood in relation to a herd, especially when they are grazing or ranging freely rather than being confined. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 14:23. That reference identifies its sole occurrence, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain its specific force there.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Adina” or “Athina.” It functions as a personal designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:42. Because the verse text is not included here, the name itself identifies the person but does not establish additional details about that person or the surrounding event.

This word means “ancient.” It is a noun used to refer to something associated with great age or the distant past. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 4:22. Because the verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that passage cannot be described further; its basic sense remains a reference to what is ancient rather than something recent or newly established.

This adjective means perpetual: continuing without end or interruption. It describes something enduring rather than temporary or short-lived. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in Wisdom and once in 4 Maccabees. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided, the word’s precise force in either passage cannot be explained beyond this central sense. Its basic emphasis is lasting permanence.

This adjective means “without authority,” describing someone or something that lacks recognized power, rightful control, or authorization. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, both times in Proverbs. The word therefore points to the absence of legitimate authority rather than simply weakness or inability. Its occurrences are in Proverbs 1:25 and Proverbs 5:7, though the precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This is a proper name, rendered “Amasai” or “Amase.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, and all three occurrences are in 1 Chronicles. Because personal names function chiefly to identify individuals, their precise significance in any one passage comes from the surrounding verse and narrative rather than from a general definition of the name itself.

Amori means “Amori,” functioning as a proper name rather than a general description or action. It identifies a named entity, but the available lexical information does not establish further details about that entity. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 9:1. The name’s precise referent and significance in that verse require the surrounding verse text and passage context, which are not included here.

Sinless describes someone or something without sin. It is an adjective used to identify a person as free from wrongdoing rather than to describe an action, place, or object. In this Greek LXX corpus, the word occurs three times, appearing once in Deuteronomy and twice in 2 Maccabees. Its central meaning remains simple and direct: the one described is not guilty of sin. The surrounding verse determines how that description functions in each passage.

This noun refers to shaking violently—an intense, forceful trembling or jolting. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nahum 2:11, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. The word describes the action or condition of being violently shaken, rather than naming a person, place, or object. Its precise force in Nahum depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to “range against” or “oppose” someone or something. It describes taking a position against another, rather than merely being separate or different. As an action word, it can express active resistance or opposition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across six verses, including passages in 1 Kings, Esther, Proverbs, and Hosea. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the subject is opposing.

Aoue, also rendered Aue, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Ezra 8, identifying the same named person or designation within that passage. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the name’s precise identity and role cannot be explained further. Its meaning is therefore its function as a personal name: it identifies someone called Aoue or Aue.

This adjective means “forbidden,” describing something that is not permitted or allowed. It presents the matter as restricted rather than open for ordinary use or discussion. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 13:22. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains clear: something prohibited or kept from being permitted.

This noun means “irreverence,” referring to a lack of reverence or honor toward God. It names an attitude or conduct rather than an individual person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 52 times, showing that the term is used repeatedly rather than being limited to one isolated passage. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains irreverence—conduct that does not show due honor.

This Greek LXX verb means “well-pleased,” expressing a favorable or satisfied response. It describes someone being pleased with what has happened or with a situation before them. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Samuel 6:19. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a positive response of satisfaction or approval.

Achilouth, also rendered Akhiluth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or named individual in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 2 Samuel 20:24. Because no surrounding verse text or additional occurrences are provided here, the name’s specific identity must be understood from that passage rather than from the name itself.

Baithēlberith, also rendered Vethilverith, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Judges 9—at Judges 9:46 and Judges 9:50. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise reference cannot be explained further here; its established lexical role is simply the name Baithēlberith or Vethilverith.

Beelsepphōn, also rendered Veelsepfon, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. As a name, it identifies a specific person, place, or other named subject rather than expressing a general quality or action. This word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus 14:2, Exodus 14:9, and Numbers 33:7. The available lexical information identifies the name itself, but the surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what named subject it identifies in each passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “pedestal,” referring to a raised support or base. It names a physical structure rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 46 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is established across many passages. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and context.

This verb means “marry”: to enter into marriage with someone. It describes the act of taking or joining a spouse, rather than naming the husband, wife, or marriage itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Genesis and Deuteronomy, so its basic meaning is clear even though it is not common in this corpus. The surrounding passage determines who is marrying and what circumstances are involved, but the word itself expresses the act of marrying.

This Greek LXX noun refers to sweetness or sweet wine. It can describe something pleasant in taste, especially a sweet drink, while its exact sense depends on the sentence where it appears. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here: twice in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. It appears in Nehemiah 8:10, Proverbs 16:24, and Sirach 11:3. These occurrences support the ordinary idea of sweetness, whether understood as a taste or as sweet wine.

This LXX Greek noun means “money lent; loan.” It refers to money given to another person with the expectation that it will be repaid, rather than to a gift or ordinary possession. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 29:4. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s exact force in that sentence must be understood from its context, but its basic meaning is a loan or money lent.

This word means “in the evening.” It is an adjective that describes something as belonging to or occurring during the evening part of the day. In the LXX corpus, it appears seven times, from Genesis through Susanna. Its use can mark the time associated with an action or event, while the precise force in a particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence. The central idea remains simple: it identifies something as evening-time.

This verb means to move thoroughly—to shift or stir something fully rather than merely touch or adjust it. It describes an action involving substantial movement, though the precise force in its single occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:23. Its basic sense remains focused on carrying out movement in a complete or thorough way.

This verb means “fall away” or “slip away.” It describes a person or thing moving away from a place, position, or condition rather than remaining where it was. As a verb, it expresses the action of departing, falling off, or losing one’s former standing. It occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, so its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This verb means “put through; make,” describing an action that causes something to be made or carried through. As a verb, it expresses what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 84 times, so its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “spear-bearing,” describing a person associated with carrying or bearing a spear. It identifies someone by this armed function rather than expressing an action or abstract quality. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek LXX corpus, with most occurrences in 4 Maccabees and one in 2 Maccabees. Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene.

This word is a personal name, referring to Ezekel, also rendered Ezekil. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 24:16. Because it is a proper name rather than a descriptive word, its meaning is primarily the identification of a person, not an action, quality, or object. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s role there.

This verb means “draw in”: to pull or bring someone or something inward. It describes an action of moving something toward the inside rather than leaving it outside. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 19:10, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular action there. The word functions as an active verb, expressing the act of drawing in or bringing inward.

This verb means to “bring out/forth” or “carry out.” It describes taking something or someone outward, bringing it forth, or carrying something away or through an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly for bringing things into view, taking them outside, or carrying out what is required. The word occurs 79 times in the LXX corpus, mostly in Old Testament books, so its precise force depends on what is being brought out or carried in each passage.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an elephant or to ivory, the valuable material associated with that animal. Its basic meaning is physical and concrete rather than a description of a person, action, or spiritual quality. In this corpus, it occurs three times, appearing in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines whether the word points directly to elephants or to ivory as a material. [p03:word:lxx:L704437:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L704437:occurrences]

This word is a proper noun identifying someone called “Hellēnis” or “Ellinis.” It is a personal designation rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 6:8. The reference locates its only occurrence, but the verse text is needed to explain what this person does or how the name functions in that passage.

This verb means to change or alter something. It describes making something different from its former state, whether by modifying it, replacing part of it, or causing a noticeable difference. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 3 Maccabees 3:21. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains the act of changing or altering. It is not a word for merely observing a difference; it expresses an action that brings about change.

This noun means “shewing forth; making known”: it refers to the act of displaying something so that it becomes evident or recognized. The idea is outward disclosure rather than something remaining hidden. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:10. Its precise emphasis in that passage depends on the surrounding text, but its basic sense remains an open showing or making known.

Epiphi, also rendered Epifi, is a proper name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 3 Maccabees 6:38. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not identify its referent or provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more about what it denotes. Its precise significance therefore depends on the context of that passage. [p03:word:lxx:L705324:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L705324:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L705324:reference:0]

This adjective describes the “highest mysteries,” pointing to matters regarded as belonging to the most elevated or profound level of mystery. As an adjective, it qualifies a person, thing, or subject by associating it with those highest mysteries rather than naming the mystery itself. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 5:13. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to be at enmity or to be hostile toward someone. It describes active opposition rather than simple disagreement, expressing a condition of hostility between parties. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs three times, so it is an uncommon word there. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains being opposed to or in conflict with another.

Zabadia, also rendered Zavathia, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies people rather than describing an action, quality, or object, so its main function is as a name within genealogical and military records. This name appears three times in the Greek LXX, all in 1 Chronicles: 8:15, 8:17, and 12:8. The supplied lexical information gives the name itself, but does not provide a further ordinary meaning or explanation of its name-origin.

It is a noun for “emulation” or “imitation”—the effort to resemble or follow another. The word points to a person’s tendency to copy, model, or match someone else, whether the emphasis is on the act of imitation or the desire behind it. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times, appearing three times in Numbers and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Thaglathphellasar” or “Thaglathfellasar.” These are two Greek renderings of the same name in the Septuagint, rather than separate ideas or qualities. It occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Kings and 2 Chronicles. The name itself identifies the person; its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “wonderful.” It describes something remarkable and deserving of amazement or admiration. It can function as an adjective, describing a person, deed, work, or other thing, and it can also be used as a noun referring to what is wonderful. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 35 times, including passages from Exodus, Deuteronomy, Job, Psalms, and several other books. Its normal meaning remains centered on something wonderful or extraordinary, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described.

This verb means “crush”: to press or break something down by force. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 10 times, including nine Old Testament occurrences and one in the deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being crushed and the surrounding sentence.

Idouram, also rendered Ithuram, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies one individual and appears only once, in 1 Chronicles 18:10. Because names primarily identify people, its significance here is the person it names, not a general concept that can be applied elsewhere. The surrounding verse provides the specific context for that individual’s appearance.

Ἰεχονίας is a proper name, rendered “Iechonias” or “Iekhonias.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. This name occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, with occurrences concentrated especially in Jeremiah. The name also appears in historical and genealogical passages. Its significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named there.

Iōnan is a proper name, rendered in the supplied lexical information as “Iōnan” or “Ionan.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs nine times, eight of them in Jonah and once in 3 Maccabees. The name appears repeatedly throughout the account of Jonah, including Jonah 1:1, 1:7, 1:15, 2:1, 2:11, and 3:1. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

This adverb means “arm fully” or “equip,” describing an action carried out with complete preparation or weaponry. It tells how someone is equipped or made ready, rather than naming the person, object, or equipment itself. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 3 Maccabees 5:23. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the context. Its central idea remains thorough equipping or full arming.

Karmēlon, also rendered Karmilon, is a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. Its meaning is therefore tied to the named person or place identified by each passage, not to a general quality or action. This Greek LXX word occurs five times in the Old Testament Greek text, across 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, and Jeremiah. The surrounding verse is needed to identify precisely what the name designates in each occurrence.

This adjective means “monthly,” describing something connected with or occurring once each month. It identifies a regular time-related pattern rather than a person, action, or object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 4:17. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what it describes there, but the word’s basic sense remains a monthly or month-related designation.

The word means “goal” or “end”: it names the point toward which something reaches or the concluding point itself. As a noun, it refers to an outcome or endpoint rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 18:7, so its wider range of use cannot be established from repeated appearances. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun means “dwelling” or “inhabiting”—the condition or act of living in a place. It points to residence or settled presence rather than movement through an area. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 106:36, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains clear: making a place one’s dwelling or living there.

Kedēmōth, also rendered Kethimoth, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named place or person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 13:18. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be explained further here; however, the lexical meaning is the name itself, not a broader descriptive term.

This verb means “sleep” or “encamp,” describing lying down to rest or staying in a camp. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for ordinary resting and for dwelling in a place, so its exact sense depends on the sentence. The word occurs eight times across eight verses, including passages from Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Psalms, Jeremiah, Zephaniah, and Song of Songs. It can therefore refer either to nighttime rest or to lodging and settlement.

This adjective means “slit-nosed,” describing someone whose nose has a cleft or narrow split. It is a physical description rather than a name for a person or an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 21:18. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain how the description functions in that specific passage, but the word itself points plainly to the shape or condition of the nose.

This adjective describes something as better, stronger in standing, or more dominant than another. It expresses comparison, indicating that one person, condition, or choice has greater advantage or superiority. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 11 times, including passages in Exodus, Judges, Psalms, Proverbs, Sirach, 1 Maccabees, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what is being compared.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Loōmim” or “Loomim.” It functions as a name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only once, in Genesis 25:3. The available form identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse determines whom or what the name identifies in that passage. It should therefore be understood as a named designation, not expanded into an abstract meaning or translated as an ordinary descriptive term.

This word means “patience”: the steady endurance that does not quickly give up or react harshly. It is a noun describing a quality a person may show while waiting, suffering, or dealing with difficulty. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs five times, across Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “superficiality,” describing what lacks depth, substance, or lasting value. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 54 times, especially in Ecclesiastes and Psalms. Its repeated use in Ecclesiastes fits language about the fleeting and insubstantial character of earthly life, while its appearances in Psalms show that the word can also describe what proves empty or unreliable before God. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being called superficial, but the central idea remains something lacking true weight or enduring substance.

Mesulam is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It does not function as a common word describing an object, action, or quality. The name appears twelve times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, especially in Ezra and Nehemiah, where it identifies individuals listed in those books. Its precise referent depends on the particular genealogy or list in which the name occurs.

This noun means “metropolis,” referring to a chief or mother city. It identifies a prominent city in relation to surrounding towns or settlements. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses, especially in Joshua, and also appears in 2 Samuel, Esther, and Isaiah. The word describes a city’s central or leading status, rather than simply any inhabited place. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a principal city.

This verb means “mimic”: to imitate or copy someone or something. It describes an action rather than a person, expressing the act of reproducing another’s manner or behavior. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines what is being imitated and why. The word’s identity and explicit definition support “mimic” as its central meaning.

Michaia, also rendered Mikhea, is a personal name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies people named Michaia in the biblical narrative and records. The name occurs 16 times in 15 verses, appearing most often in Judges and also in 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. Its exact significance in any individual passage comes from the surrounding context and the person being named.

This word means “little calf,” referring to a young cow or bull. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament for an animal, including calves presented in sacrificial settings and calves prepared as food. The word occurs 12 times in 12 Old Testament verses, from Genesis through Malachi. Its ordinary meaning remains specific and concrete: a young bovine animal, rather than a general word for livestock or sacrifice.

Neesthan is a proper name preserved as “Neesthan” in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object; its role is to identify a particular named entity. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 18:4. The name’s specific reference and significance must be understood from that passage’s actual wording and surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means “perception,” referring to the mind’s awareness or grasp of something. It names an inner act of recognizing or taking in what is presented, rather than an outward action. The word occurs twice in the deuterocanonical Greek writings, in Baruch and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence. Ogotholia is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular named entity, but the available lexical information does not specify whether that entity is a person, place, or something else. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 8:26. Its precise referent must therefore be understood from that passage’s surrounding text rather than from the name alone.

This noun means “little awl,” a small pointed tool used for piercing or making a hole. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, in Exodus 21:6 and Deuteronomy 15:17. Its ordinary meaning identifies the physical instrument itself rather than an action, person, or quality. The word therefore refers to a specific hand tool, with the surrounding verse determining how that tool is being used in its sentence.

This adjective means “all-seeing”: it describes one who sees everything or is aware of all things. It presents comprehensive sight or awareness rather than limited human observation. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:5. The reference identifies where it appears, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular force there. Its basic meaning remains a description of complete sight or awareness.

This verb means “cast along” or “set against.” It describes an action of placing or throwing something alongside or opposite something else. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, appearing especially in Proverbs and also in Ruth and 2 Maccabees. Its exact sense in any particular verse depends on what is being placed, thrown, or set against what. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality.

This verb means “drift aside”: to move away from a proper path, position, or course rather than remain steady. It presents movement that slips or wanders from where it should be. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Proverbs 3:21 and Isaiah 44:4, so its normal sense is focused and specific rather than broadly varied. The surrounding verse determines what is drifting and what direction or standard it is departing from.

This word describes a resident or foreigner—someone living in a place without being regarded as a native member of that community. It can refer to a person dwelling among another people or residing in a land that is not understood as his permanent homeland. As an adjective, it describes that status or condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 23 times, showing repeated use for people living among others as non-natives.

This verb means “plant round about,” describing the act of setting plants around something or arranging them in a surrounding growth. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 2:21. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is planting in an encircling or surrounding arrangement.

This verb means to lame or maim—to cause someone or something to lose normal physical ability through injury. It describes an action rather than a person or condition, so its sentence role is to express what is done to another. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 18:21. That reference identifies its location, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the specific situation there.

This verb means “pass the sea”—to travel across or through the sea. It describes an action rather than a person or object, showing what someone is doing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 30:19. Its central idea is movement across the sea; the precise force of that action in the verse depends on the surrounding passage. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that Greek Old Testament setting.

This Greek LXX verb means “address”: to speak to or call someone by a name or title. It describes the act of directing speech toward a person, rather than merely mentioning them. The word occurs seven times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Deuteronomy and six times in later deuterocanonical writings. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on whom the speaker addresses and why, but its central sense remains the direct act of addressing someone.

To prophesy means to speak a prophetic message. This Greek LXX verb describes the act of declaring what is presented as a message from God, rather than merely offering a personal opinion. It is used 114 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, showing a recurring biblical action associated with prophetic speech. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the act of prophesying.

This Greek LXX verb means “trade” or “sell”: to exchange goods or property for something of value. It describes the act of offering something in commerce or transferring it to another person through a sale. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, including passages involving food, land, servants, and merchandise. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being exchanged and the surrounding sentence.

This word means “dragnet,” a large net used to gather fish. It is a noun referring to the fishing equipment itself, rather than the act of fishing or the people who fish. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, including passages in Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Habakkuk. Its normal meaning remains centered on a net drawn through the water to collect fish.

Samagoth is a proper name, referring to a specific person or place rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Jeremiah 46:3. The available rendering preserves the name as “Samagoth,” matching the supplied meaning “Samagōth; Samagoth.” Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that passage cannot be described further.

Serran is a proper name, identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 23:9. Since the available wording gives only the name itself and no surrounding verse text, its precise identity and role must be determined from that passage. The name should therefore be understood simply as “Serran,” a personal designation preserved in this one Old Testament occurrence.

Sirdatha is a proper name, given in the alternate form “Sirthatha.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 4:17. The available information establishes the name and its spelling forms, but the verse text is needed to determine exactly whom or what the name identifies in that passage.

Emerald is a noun naming a precious green stone. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it refers to the gemstone itself, including its use among valuable stones associated with sacred clothing and furnishings. The word occurs eight times in this LXX corpus, appearing especially in Exodus and also in Ezekiel and Sirach. Its basic meaning remains the name of this distinctive gemstone.

This Greek LXX verb means “drop” or “drip.” It describes liquid falling in drops or being released gradually, rather than pouring out all at once. As a verb, it expresses the action itself. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Micah 2:11; the precise force of the word there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic idea remains the falling or dripping of liquid.

This Greek LXX verb means to “feed with” or “graze with,” describing animals sharing pasture or feeding alongside one another. It expresses joint feeding rather than merely eating, so the word focuses on creatures being together as they graze. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 11:6, and its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.
